changed_views: The August 11 Chai interview supported a pure software-and-model business. Jaderberg makes Isomorphic's contrasting choice explicit: retain the engine and pursue owned and partnered therapeutics. The companies need different commercial and capital-efficiency comparisons even if their modeling capabilities overlap.

Refine the meaning of vertical integration at Isomorphic: core models and proprietary data are strategic assets, while experimental work can involve CROs and specialist platforms. Laboratory ownership alone is an incomplete proxy for its data advantage.

The earlier AlphaFold and Biohub coverage's clinical-evidence boundary remains intact. Internal experimental-accuracy targets and clinical hiring do not yet demonstrate lower human failure rates, and this interview adds no dated first-trial commitment.
follow_ups: Track named internal and partnered candidates, trial registry identifiers, sponsor responsibilities, first-patient dosing and human safety/efficacy readouts. Separate preparation and trial registration from actual enrollment.

Compare Isomorphic's owned-pipeline and collaboration economics with Chai's platform strategy using disclosed upfront payments, milestones, royalties, retained rights and development spending; do not equate model quality with recurring software margins.

Request prospective, held-out results for the experimental-accuracy targets: endpoints, error tolerances, calibration, unseen targets or modalities, number of synthesized compounds, failed predictions, and elapsed laboratory time against an explicit baseline.

Look for quantitative evidence behind the claimed data-scaling behavior: dataset composition, experimental selection policy, negative results, data rights and transfer to new programs after controlling for target similarity.

For human-toxicity modeling, require a defined endpoint and intended regulatory use, human-label provenance, external validation and prospective performance. Track actual regulator acceptance of a specific method separately from general NAMs policy.

signals.claim: Jaderberg says Isomorphic does not sell or license its model: it uses the engine internally for fully owned drug programs and joint programs with pharma, with its own pipeline focused on oncology, immunology and inflammation.
signals.evidence: At 26:27 he explicitly excludes model licensing and token sales; at 26:38 he distinguishes programs Isomorphic funds and owns from partnered projects. At 27:23 he names its internal therapeutic focus while describing the engine as disease-, target-class- and modality-agnostic. The latter is a capability claim without a cross-domain benchmark in this interview. Isomorphic's [partnership page](https://www.isomorphiclabs.com/partnerships) corroborates program-based collaborations with Novartis, Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson. The business implication is exposure to therapeutic development and partnership economics; no new contract terms or realized returns are disclosed.

signals.claim: Jaderberg says Isomorphic benchmarks its predictive models against experimental accuracy and aims to use physical experiments increasingly for validation, reducing the number of laboratory iterations needed for design.
signals.evidence: At 16:47 he describes experimental accuracy as a target drawn on internal leaderboards. At 24:45 he says Isomorphic already uses automated labs, but reaction and cell-culture times motivate moving more iteration onto computers; at 26:01 he retains real-world safety and hypothesis validation. He supplies no numerical error tolerance or measured cycle reduction here. Separate evidence: the company's [February IsoDDE report summary](https://www.isomorphiclabs.com/articles/the-isomorphic-labs-drug-design-engine-unlocks-a-new-frontier) reports structure, binding-affinity and pocket-prediction results. Its [September demonstration](https://www.isomorphiclabs.com/articles/building-a-new-path-to-make-medicines-with-ai) describes computational searches over 2–4 days followed by laboratory testing of selected compounds. These support narrower modeling and laboratory claims, without establishing clinical safety or end-to-end development acceleration.

signals.claim: Jaderberg says Isomorphic deliberately generates proprietary data with distributions suited to generalization, because historical public and pharma repositories can be biased by the drug programs that produced them.
signals.evidence: At 19:49 he describes much existing data as the passive byproduct of medicine development; at 20:17 he argues that general models need a different data distribution and reports favorable data-scaling behavior from self-generated data. At 23:16 he says model development is entirely internal while experiments use a mix of internal work, CROs and specialist companies, with proprietary data ownership an objective. No dataset sizes, scaling curves, acquisition costs or held-out performance numbers are given. The useful distinction is between owning the model/data asset and owning every experimental platform; durable cross-program transfer remains a claim to test.

signals.claim: Jaderberg proposes combining in-vitro measurements, organoids or organ-on-chip systems and AI models to predict human toxicity more directly, while acknowledging that human clinical labels are scarce.
signals.evidence: At 21:49–22:46 he describes a proposed human-relevant prediction stack and the limited number of clinical trials available for training. The interview supplies no endpoint-level accuracy, prospective validation or evidence that Isomorphic has replaced a required safety study. His numerical characterization of rat-to-human predictivity lacks a named study. Regulatory context is more specific than a blanket requirement for animal tests: the FDA says it reviews scientifically valid NAMs, and its [March 2026 draft guidance announcement](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-releases-draft-guidance-alternatives-animal-testing-drug-development) sets out context-of-use, human-relevance, reproducibility and fitness-for-purpose principles. The [guidance remains draft and nonbinding](https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/general-considerations-use-new-approach-methodologies-drug-development); this does not establish acceptance of an Isomorphic method.

signals.claim: Asked when Isomorphic will begin its first clinical trial, Jaderberg declines to give a date and says the clinical-development team is being built; his five-year expectation concerns better predictive tools, not a specified cure rate.
signals.evidence: At 34:26–34:47 he responds to the first-trial question with frontier-science uncertainty and hiring progress. At 35:01 he expects a large improvement in biological prediction and molecule design within five years, while acknowledging that development still takes years. He does not adopt Elad Gil's proposed 80%-of-cancers metric or supply human results. Isomorphic's [September 29 update](https://www.isomorphiclabs.com/articles/building-a-new-path-to-make-medicines-with-ai) likewise describes preclinical data and preparation for clinical development. The transcript supports organizational readiness work, but does not identify a candidate, trial registration, first patient dosed or demonstrated clinical advantage.

summary: Max Jaderberg clarifies Isomorphic Labs' operating model: keep the drug-design engine in house, generate proprietary training data, and use the models across wholly owned and partnered drug programs. Its internal research target is experimental accuracy, with computation reducing physical design-test iterations. He describes a clinical-development team buildout but declines to date the first trial. The interview adds useful strategic detail, while providing no new quantitative benchmark, prospective human-toxicity validation or clinical efficacy result. Timestamps refer to the official YouTube edition.
why_it_matters: Isomorphic's returns depend on drug-program progress and retained therapeutic economics, making pipeline milestones, partnership terms and clinical execution central to assessing its AI advantage. Its data strategy also makes experimental design and ownership material competitive variables. Compared with prior coverage of Chai's software-platform strategy and Biohub's measurement infrastructure, this interview clarifies a different route to capturing value from biological models. It does not establish that predictive gains have reduced clinical failure rates.
